questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Environment as a Political Question' refers to.
questions.a: Environmental concerns entered world politics as the effects of industrial growth - ozone depletion, global warming, resource depletion - crossed borders; since northern states industrialised first, questions of responsibility and equity divide rich and developing countries.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Environment as a Political Question'.
questions.a: The core clash is distributive: who bears the cost of saving a commons damaged mostly by the industrialised North?

questions.q: Under which section is 'Environment as a Political Question' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Environmental Concerns in Global Politics (source: leps106.txt environmental concerns and North-South divides sections)

Explain in your own words what 'Global Commons and Conferences' refers to.
questions.a: The global commons - earth's atmosphere, Antarctica, ocean floor and outer space - lie outside national jurisdiction; the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 reserved the continent for peaceful science, and conferences from Stockholm 1972 to Rio 1992 and Kyoto 1997 built the regime of environmental agreements.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Global Commons and Conferences'.
questions.a: The Kyoto protocol followed the Rio earth summit by the difference of 1997 and 1992.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Global Commons and Conferences', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Indigenous Peoples and Resource Rights' refers to.
questions.a: Indigenous peoples - whose homelands cross borders and whose cultures predate modern states - seek recognition of land and resource rights; their movements highlight how states and corporations appropriate forests, minerals and knowledge, and the UN declared an international day and decade for them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Indigenous Peoples and Resource Rights'.
questions.a: Indigenous claims turn environment into justice: protecting cultures means protecting the ecosystems they manage.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Indigenous Peoples and Resource Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Indigenous Peoples and their Rights (source: leps106.txt indigenous peoples' definition, voices and rights sections)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Resource Geopolitics: Oil and Water' refers to.
questions.a: Resources shape world politics: oil concentrates power in West Asia and the control of supply lines, and water - river basins like the Jordan, Tigris-Euphrates and the Indus - generates disputes where upstream and downstream states meet; competition for natural resources remains a driver of conflict.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Resource Geopolitics: Oil and Water'.
questions.a: Whoever commands pipelines, straits and river heads commands leverage: resource geography is power geography.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Resource Geopolitics: Oil and Water' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Resource Geopolitics (source: leps106.txt oil politics, water disputes and regional competition sections)
